query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In the dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing, high-temperature oxidation induces a localized redistribution of elements, particularly leading to the enrichment of oxidation‐resistant species (e.g., Cr and Ti) at the nanoprecipitate/matrix and oxide interfaces, which may enhance the formation of a protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA possessing dual nanoprecipitates that contribute to a 300–400 MPa strength improvement over cast/wrought versions.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., around 1000°C in air) under controlled durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in an air environment with varied oxidation times to capture early and later stages of oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoprecipitates and their interfaces with the surrounding matrix.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, atomic diffusion leads to elemental redistribution; oxidation‐resistant elements such as Cr and Ti are hypothesized to segregate to the nanoprecipitate interfaces and at the oxide/matrix boundary, facilitating the formation of a dense, protective oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) will reveal sub-nanometer scale gradients in elemental composition, notably showing higher local concentrations of Cr and Ti around the nanoprecipitates in oxidized samples compared to the unoxidized control, thereby correlating elemental segregation with improved oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: Unoxidized additive-manufactured HEA samples exhibiting a relatively uniform element distribution within nanoprecipitates.
generation.boundary: The exact temperature, oxidation duration thresholds, and quantitative extent of elemental enrichment are uncertain, and contributions from secondary phases or minor elements may also affect the oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the rate, magnitude, and stability over time of the elemental segregation, as well as its precise effect on long-term oxidation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples via additive manufacturing. Subject a set of samples to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 1000°C in air) for various durations while keeping a control set unoxidized. Utilize ex situ Atom Probe Tomography (APT) to obtain three-dimensional elemental maps at sub-nanometer resolution, focusing on the nanoprecipitate regions and their interfaces.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of Cr and Ti concentrations at nanoprecipitate/matrix and oxide interfaces
Comparative analysis of oxide thickness and morphology using complementary electron microscopy techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT analysis does not reveal a statistically significant enrichment of oxidation-resistant elements (Cr, Ti) at the nanoprecipitate interfaces or within the emergent oxide scale in the oxidized samples relative to the unoxidized control, then the hypothesis fails. In other words, a lack of measurable elemental redistribution would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. decision.trend: Prior studies on high-entropy alloys for high-temperature applications show a strong focus on improving oxidation resistance through microstructural refinement, composition tuning, and protective coatings. In 2022 (PMC9026100), an ultrafine-grain AlCoCrFeNi HEA was processed via friction methods and exhibited improved oxidation behavior, but the distribution of key oxide-forming elements at the nanoscale was not fully detailed. In 2023 (PMC10142552), researchers systematically varied Cr content in WVTaTiCrx HEA coatings to understand its effect on oxidation resistance, primarily using conventional oxidation and microstructure analyses. By 2024 (PMC11077685), silicide coatings were added to HfNbTaTiZr HEA for enhanced oxidation resistance, yet an in-depth mechanistic understanding of how nanoprecipitates specifically contribute to oxidation protection remained largely unexplored. Across these works, standard approaches (isothermal oxidation tests, electron microscopy, surface analyses) helped measure kinetics and oxidation products but did not fully reveal the atomic-level pathways of elemental redistribution in nanoprecipitates during high-temperature exposure.
decision.unsolved: A fundamental, high-resolution understanding of how nanoprecipitates redistribute elements during oxidation remains elusive. Important questions persist about the local elemental transport at the oxide–matrix interface and how precipitates evolve or dissolve under oxidizing conditions. Addressing these gaps is crucial for tailoring precipitation strategies in additive-manufactured HEAs for enhanced high-temperature durability.
decision.lever: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) on ex situ or in situ oxidized samples to track the 3D elemental distribution at sub-nanometer resolution around nanoprecipitates
decision.why: Building on standard oxidation and microstructural investigations, APT provides a direct means to elucidate how each constituent migrates during oxidation. This 3D atomic-scale analysis is essential for clarifying precipitation evolution, interfacial segregation, and oxide scale formation mechanisms, which are all key to improving long-term oxidation resistance in additive-manufactured high-entropy alloys.
